source: A one-degree slip in the angle changes the height by an amount that grows fast at steep angles. Choosing the baseline well keeps the error small.
Students assume the error in height is the same whatever the angle.

From the story. The boys' theodolites were homemade, so every angle they read came with some uncertainty. A good scientist reports how far off the answer might be, not just the answer. (More in October Sky.)

Suppose the angle could be off by $\pm 2^\circ$. The true height is somewhere between $b\tan(\theta - 2^\circ)$ and $b\tan(\theta + 2^\circ)$. Because the tangent climbs steeply near $90^\circ$, the same $2^\circ$ slip matters much more at steep angles.

Height range: $b\tan(\theta - \Delta\theta) \le h \le b\tan(\theta + \Delta\theta)$. With calculus, $dh = b\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ ($d\theta$ in radians), so the relative error $\dfrac{dh}{h} = \dfrac{d\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}$ is smallest at $\theta = 45^\circ$. Two or three trackers in different directions, averaged, cancel some of the error from a rocket that drifted.
The gold wedge is $\pm 2^\circ$. Watch the red band of possible heights stretch as the angle climbs.
A tracker $100\ \text{m}$ away reads $70^\circ \pm 2^\circ$. Give the range of heights.
So $h$ is between about $248$ and $308\ \text{m}$, a spread of $60\ \text{m}$. At $45^\circ \pm 2^\circ$ the spread would be only about $14\ \text{m}$.
Assuming a fixed angle error gives a fixed height error. It depends strongly on the angle.
